description: We are NABA', four participants from Cairo combining data analysis, backend, design and storytelling. Our goal is to make NISAR radar data easy for everyone to understand, through an interactive map and an immersive VR experience that show how fires and wetlands change over time.
summary:
Naba (نبأ, Arabic for “news”) is a newsroom for the Earth. It turns measurements from NISAR, the new NASA–ISRO L-band radar satellite, into short news stories on an interactive 3D globe. Each story gives a headline, a place, one measured number, a chart over time, possible causes, why it matters, and what to check next.
Radar sees through cloud and smoke, day and night, but its images are hard for non-specialists to read. Our Python pipeline, covered by 51 automated tests, streams only the small part of each NISAR product that covers a site, measures the change, and writes it as a plain-language story. Today Naba shows seven measured stories: a magnitude 7.7 earthquake in Panama, two wildfire burn scars in the USA, and wetland water changes at Lake Manzala (Egypt), the Okavango Delta (Botswana) and the Everglades (USA).
For the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, Naba makes SAR data understandable to the public, journalists, teachers and local decision makers, starting with Egypt’s own Nile Delta.
details:
What it does

Naba turns NISAR radar measurements into news. Open the site and you see a dark 3D globe with coloured pins. Each pin is a story about a real place where NISAR measured a change.

Click a pin and the globe flies there. A panel shows the headline, the measured number, a chart with one point per radar pass, what is happening, possible causes (as possibilities, never as proof), why it matters, and what to check next.

A slider steps through the radar passes or months, and “Compare dates” puts radar images from two dates side by side.

Try it (main task)

1.    Open the website. Watch the 24-second narrated intro, or skip it.

2.    Take the guided tour. It shows an earthquake (Panama), a flood pulse (Okavango) and a wildfire (Big Sur) in under a minute.

3.    Click the red pin in California (“Radar maps a burn scar of about 31 km² in Big Sur”).

4.    Drag the slider from 16 August to 15 October and watch the burn scar appear pass by pass.

5.    Press “Compare dates” to see the radar false-colour image before and after the fire.

Direct link to one story: add /?story=plaskett-burn-scar to the site URL. Add /?demo=1 to autoplay the main path.

How it works

1.    Search. The Python pipeline (naba-data) queries NASA’s Common Metadata Repository for NISAR products over a site and period. Only metadata moves.

2.    Select. It keeps dual-polarisation (HH + HV) passes from one track, direction and frame, so every date is seen from the same angle and brightness can be compared.

3.    Stream. Each NISAR product is 4–6 GB. Naba uses HTTPS range requests to read only the HDF5 chunks over the site. For the two fires it read about 252 MB out of about 61 GB of products (0.4%). Every subset is cached as a GeoTIFF, so a re-run downloads nothing.

4.    Measure. Wetlands: each pixel is classed as open water (dark in HH and HV), flooded vegetation (bright HH, large HH−HV gap) or other, then composited per month. Fires: the HV signal of every pass is compared with the last pass before the fire; a drop of more than 3 dB is “likely burned” and 2–3 dB is “possibly burned”. Earthquakes: the unwrapped interferogram phase is converted to centimetres of ground motion along the satellite’s line of sight, keeping only pixels with coherence of 0.3 or more.

5.    Map. Class masks are turned into polygons with areas measured on the WGS84 ellipsoid, plus image frames for “Compare dates”.

6.    Tell. Each measurement is written as a story from fixed templates filled with the measured numbers. No language model writes the stories. Every number is traceable in provenance.json, which lists every granule, threshold, date and megabyte used.

The seven measured stories

 

Tools and languages

•     Web app: TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS 5 (globe projection), Zustand, lucide-react icons.

•     Data pipeline: Python with earthaccess, h5py, fsspec/aiohttp, xarray, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, rasterio, pyproj, Shapely and Pillow. 51 automated tests (pytest) cover thresholds, burn tiers, polygon areas, story format and dataset merging; all pass.

•     Mixed reality (extra): Unity 6 with the Meta XR SDK, OpenXR and URP, for Meta Quest 3S. The same stories float on a globe in your room; tapping one unrolls it into a flat map with the radar layer.

Benefits and goals

•     Makes SAR readable by anyone: one headline, one number and a plain explanation, instead of a raw radar image.

•     Works when optical satellites cannot: through cloud, smoke and darkness.

•     Honest by design: every story lists causes as possibilities and says what to check next. Radar burn areas are shown next to the officially reported fire size.

•     Cheap to run: no backend, no API keys, and only the needed part of each product is read.

What works now, limits and next steps

Works now: the website with globe, story panel, charts, slider, Compare dates, narrated intro and guided tour, all seven stories measured from real NISAR data, the reproducible pipeline with its 51 passing tests, and the Quest version (built from the repo in Unity). All of it is in the public repo.

Limits: NISAR data is still PROVISIONAL. The wetland and burn classes are exploratory dB thresholds, not validated flood or burn-severity maps; wind on water, wet soil and look angle can move the numbers, so no story claims high confidence. Because only clear drops in the radar signal count as burned, the Big Sur scar we measure (31 km² likely burned) is well below the 121 km² reported fire. For the same reason, we call the Lake Manzala change (2.4% to 2.6%) small rather than treating it as a trend. Earthquake motion is along the line of sight only, from one pair. The globe shows simplified outlines, not full 20 m detail. The Quest version needs a headset and Unity to build.

Next: more sites through the same pipeline (more Egyptian sites first); validation against water gauges, official fire perimeters and GPS; a FastAPI + PostGIS service serving the same data (the frontend already supports it through one setting); and tiled rasters so the globe can zoom to full resolution.

Github repo Source Code: https://github.com/AhmedAshry7/naba

Use of AI

• Stories and numbers: no AI. Every story is filled in from fixed templates using the numbers the pipeline measures. No language model writes or changes them, and every value can be traced in provenance.json.

• Coding help: we used Claude as a coding assistant on parts of the web app and pipeline. The team reviewed every change, and the 51 tests check the results.

• Narration: the intro and tour voices are AI-generated with Microsoft neural text-to-speech (edge-tts), reading lines the team wrote.
